title: Word Break
directAnswer: Can s be cut into a sequence of dictionary words? Define dp[i] = 'the prefix s[0..i) is fully segmentable'. dp[0] = true; dp[i] is true if some j < i has dp[j] true AND s[j..i) is a dictionary word. Put the dictionary in a hash set for O(1) lookup. Memoized recursion or a bottom-up dp[] both run in O(n²) (times word-length for substring/lookup).

remember.pattern: Prefix-partition DP over a hash-set dictionary
remember.formula:
wordSet = set(wordDict)
dp[0] = True
for i in 1..n:
    dp[i] = any(dp[j] and s[j:i] in wordSet for j in 0..i-1)
return dp[n]
rules: State is the **prefix boundary**: `dp[i]` = 'can `s[0..i)` be segmented into dictionary words?'
`dp[0] = true` — the empty prefix is trivially segmentable; this anchors every later state.
`dp[i]` is true iff there's a split point `j` with `dp[j]` true **and** `s[j..i)` in the dictionary — a known-good prefix plus one more word.
Store `wordDict` in a **hash set** for O(1) membership; scanning the list each time adds an O(dictSize) factor.
It's a reachability/boolean OR (`any`), not a count or a min — you only care *whether* a segmentation exists.
whenToUse: Decide whether a string splits into pieces drawn from a fixed vocabulary
A prefix is valid iff some earlier prefix is valid plus one more allowed chunk
Boolean 'is it reachable?' over positions in a sequence
Substring/segment problems where dictionary membership is O(1) via a set
antiSignals: You must return ALL segmentations → Word Break II, backtracking with memo of lists
You need the minimum number of pieces → switch boolean OR to a min count DP
The dictionary is enormous and words are long → consider a Trie to bound the inner scan
Pieces can overlap or reorder freely → not a left-to-right partition problem
remember.takeaway: Word Break is the canonical 'can this sequence be partitioned?' DP. The unlock is indexing state by a prefix boundary and asking 'is there an earlier valid cut plus one dictionary word?'. Swap the boolean for a count or a list and the same dp drives Word Break II, Palindrome Partitioning, and Concatenated Words.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you model the string as partition-by-prefix DP, recognize the overlapping subproblems that make naive recursion exponential, and use a hash set for O(1) dictionary lookups.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Greedily matching the longest (or first) word and committing to it, which fails on inputs like 'applepenapple' where an early wrong cut dooms the rest; or doing O(dictSize) list scans instead of a set.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State dp[i] precisely, explain why dp[0] = true anchors it, justify the hash set, and mention the Trie optimization and the Word Break II follow-up that returns actual segmentations.

problemStatement:
Given a string `s` and a dictionary of strings `wordDict`, return `true` if `s` can be **segmented** into a space-separated sequence of one or more dictionary words.

**Note:** the same dictionary word may be reused ***multiple times*** in the segmentation.
constraints: s and wordDict[i] consist of only lowercase English letters
All the strings of wordDict are unique
understanding: Decide whether the whole string can be chopped into consecutive chunks, each of which is a word in the dictionary, reusing words as needed. We don't need the segmentation itself — just whether one exists.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can dictionary words be reused?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — the same word may appear any number of times in the segmentation. That's why we don't remove used words.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must every character be covered?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. The segmentation must consume all of s with no leftover characters — that's what dp[n] (the full length) checks.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the dictionary large enough to matter for lookups?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 1000 words. Put them in a hash set so each membership test is O(word length), not an O(1000) list scan.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the order of words in the dictionary matter?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. We only test membership of substrings, so the dictionary is just a set.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Would a greedy longest-match work?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. On s = 'applepenapple' a greedy that grabs a wrong early chunk can strand the rest. We need DP to consider all split points.

examples.explanation: No segmentation covers the whole string — every path leaves a leftover that isn't a word.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: The decision tree to run before writing code. Word Break lands on the bottom-up prefix-DP branch.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Recursion Over Start Index
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first to establish the split-point recurrence, then flag the exponential re-exploration before optimizing.
hints: Think about where the FIRST word ends. If s[0..k) is a dictionary word, what's left to solve?
If a prefix s[start..end) is in the dictionary, recurse on the remaining suffix starting at end. Succeed if any prefix leads to a fully consumed string.
Write canBreak(start) = (start == n) OR any end>start with s[start..end) in dict AND canBreak(end).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each start index tries up to n end positions and recurses, and without caching the same suffixes are re-explored across paths → up to 2ⁿ calls. Each substring build / set lookup costs O(L) where L is word length. Stack depth O(n).
approaches.explanation:
Reason from the front. To break `s` starting at index `start`, try every prefix `s[start..end)`: if that prefix is a dictionary word, recursively try to break the remaining suffix from `end`. If any choice of `end` lets the rest of the string break cleanly, the whole thing breaks. The base case is `start == n` — we've consumed the entire string, so success.

**The mental shift: commit to one word, recurse on the suffix.** Don't try to place all the cuts at once. Just decide where the *first* word ends, then the remainder is the same problem on a shorter string. Because words can repeat, we never remove anything from the dictionary — every word is available again in the suffix.

**Why greedy fails and we must try every prefix.** A greedy 'take the longest matching word' can make a locally fine choice that strands the rest. On `"catsandog"` grabbing `"cats"` then `"and"` leaves `"og"`, dead; the only hope is exploring *all* split points, which is exactly what the `any(...)` over `end` does.

**Why we don't ship this.** Different prefixes can lead to the same suffix `start`, and the naive recursion re-solves `canBreak(start)` every time it's reached — exponential overlap. Name it, then cache by `start`.
approaches.insight: The only thing that determines whether the rest of the string breaks is the *starting index* of the suffix — the path taken to get there is irrelevant. That 'future depends only on position' property is the hallmark of a problem that memoizes into a clean polynomial DP.

edgeCases.behavior: canBreak(0): prefix "a" in dict → canBreak(1) hits start==n → true.

pitfalls: Scanning the wordDict list with contains() on a List instead of a Set — adds an O(dictSize) factor.
Greedy first/longest match — commits to a cut that can strand the rest (false negatives).
Shipping the uncached recursion — exponential, TLEs on adversarial inputs like 'aaaa...a' with dict ['a','aa'].

approaches.name: Top-Down Memoization
approaches.whenToMention: The fix once you see the overlap — 'cache canBreak(start) so each suffix is solved once'.
hints: canBreak(start) returns the same answer every time it's called. Where can you store it?
Memoize by start index. On entry, return the cached boolean if known; otherwise compute and store it.
memo[start] = any prefix word from start whose suffix also breaks; cache false results too.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are n distinct start indices. Each does an O(n) loop over end positions with an O(L) substring/lookup → O(n² · L) time. The memo plus recursion stack is O(n).
approaches.explanation:
Keep the same start-index recursion, but cache `canBreak(start)`. A `memo` array (or map) indexed by start position remembers whether the suffix from that point can be segmented, so each suffix is solved exactly once.

**The mental shift: a suffix has one verdict, independent of how you arrived.** In the brute force, the suffix beginning at index `start` might be reached via many different prefix combinations, and each time we re-explore it from scratch. Since the answer for a given `start` is fixed, caching it turns the exponential tree into n unique subproblems.

**Why caching `false` matters as much as `true`.** A suffix that *cannot* be broken (like `"og"` in `"catsandog"`) is hit repeatedly through different failing prefixes. Remembering its `false` verdict makes every later visit O(1), which is where most of the speed-up actually comes from on negative cases.

**Why the dictionary stays a set.** Membership is the inner-loop hot path. A `HashSet` keeps each `s[start..end)` lookup at O(word length); a `List.contains` would multiply the whole thing by the dictionary size.
approaches.insight: Memoization here is the textbook upgrade: a correct recursion whose state is a single integer (`start`) plus heavy overlap becomes O(states × work-per-state) the moment you add a cache. The intellectual step was realizing the start index fully determines the future — the cache is then mechanical.

dryRun.intro: memo[start] caches whether the suffix from start can be segmented. False results are remembered too.

Cache hit — return the stored verdict, including remembered failures, in O(1).
Found a working split — record success before short-circuiting out.
No split worked from here; cache the failure so this suffix is never re-explored.

pitfalls: Using primitive boolean[] (defaults to false) — can't distinguish 'uncomputed' from a cached false; use Boolean[] with null.
Caching only true results — failures are re-explored and you stay slow on negative cases.
List.contains instead of a Set — multiplies runtime by dictionary size.

approaches.name: Bottom-Up — dp[] Over Prefix Boundaries (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'dp[i] = can s[0..i) be segmented; build i from 0 up to n'.
hints: Define dp[i] = 'the first i characters can be segmented'. What's the trivially true base case?
dp[0] = true (empty prefix). For each end i, look back to every split j: if dp[j] is true and s[j..i) is a word, dp[i] is true.
Two nested loops over i (1..n) and j (0..i-1); break out as soon as one valid j is found. Answer is dp[n].
approaches.complexityReasoning: Outer loop over n end positions, inner loop over up to n split points, each doing an O(L) substring/lookup → O(n² · L) time. One dp array of size n + 1 → O(n) space, no recursion stack.
approaches.explanation:
Turn the recursion around and build verdicts for prefixes, shortest to longest. `dp[i]` means 'the prefix `s[0..i)` can be fully segmented'. Anchor `dp[0] = true` (the empty prefix needs no words). Then for each end boundary `i`, scan every earlier boundary `j`: if `dp[j]` is true *and* `s[j..i)` is a dictionary word, then `s[0..i)` splits as (a known-good prefix) + (one more word), so `dp[i] = true`. The final answer is `dp[n]`.

**The mental shift: index state by the cut position, not the character.** The hard part of segmentation is that cuts can fall anywhere. By making `dp[i]` answer 'is there *any* valid way to end a word exactly at position i?', each `dp[i]` reduces to 'is there an earlier valid cut `j` followed by a single dictionary word `s[j..i)`?'. You're gluing one word onto an already-solved shorter prefix — that's the entire recurrence.

**Why dp[0] = true is load-bearing.** Every true entry ultimately chains back to `dp[0]`: the first word of any segmentation needs `dp[0]` to be true so that `s[0..len)` can light up `dp[len]`. Leave `dp[0]` false and nothing ever becomes true — the whole table collapses to false.

**Why bottom-up needs no recursion.** Since `dp[i]` only reads `dp[j]` for `j < i`, sweeping `i` upward guarantees every dependency is already final. The dictionary lives in a hash set so each `s[j..i)` test is O(word length), and a small early `break` exits the inner loop the moment `dp[i]` is confirmed true.
approaches.insight: Word Break is the prototypical 'can this sequence be partitioned?' DP, and the dp[i] = OR over (dp[j] AND chunk valid) shape is reusable. Replace the boolean OR with a sum to count segmentations, with a min to minimize pieces, or carry back-pointers to reconstruct the actual words (Word Break II) — same prefix-boundary skeleton, different aggregation.

diagrams.title: dp over prefix boundaries
diagrams.caption: dp[i] = 'first i chars segmentable'. Cells flip true when a valid cut + word lands on i.

edgeCases.behavior: dp[3],dp[4],dp[7] light up but dp[9] never does — no word ends exactly at length 9 from a valid cut → false.
Each dp[i] becomes true via multiple j's; dp[4] = true → segmentable.

pitfalls: Forgetting dp[0] = true — nothing can ever become true and you always return false.
Returning dp[n-1] instead of dp[n] — off-by-one that ignores the last character.
Looping j over the dictionary's word lengths incorrectly, or using List.contains — keep the set and the j-over-prefixes form for clarity.
Rebuilding the set inside the loop — hash it once before the loops.

commonMistakes: Greedy longest/first match — an early wrong cut strands the rest and returns a false negative.
Using a List and List.contains for the dictionary — multiplies runtime by the dictionary size; use a HashSet.
Forgetting the dp[0] = true base case — the whole table stays false.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Greedy longest-match
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Committing to the longest matching prefix can leave an unbreakable remainder. On 'catsandog' grabbing 'cats' then 'and' leaves 'og'. Only trying ALL split points (DP) is correct.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
i = 0
while i < len(s):
    matched = max((w for w in wordDict if s.startswith(w, i)), key=len, default=None)
    if not matched:
        return False
    i += len(matched)
return True

commonMistakesDetailed.title: List lookup instead of a set
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Membership against a List is O(dictSize) per check, so the inner loop becomes O(n · dictSize). Hashing the dictionary once makes each lookup O(word length).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the dp[0] anchor
commonMistakesDetailed.why: dp[0] = true represents the empty prefix. Without it, no s[0..len) can ever set dp[len] = true, so every input returns false.

followupVariations.title: Word Break II
followupVariations.hint: Return ALL segmentations, not just whether one exists. Memoize start → list of sentences and backtrack.

followupVariations.title: Concatenated Words
followupVariations.hint: Run Word Break on each word using the others as the dictionary — find words built from two or more shorter words.

followupVariations.title: Palindrome Partitioning
followupVariations.hint: Same prefix-partition DP, but the 'dictionary check' is 'is this substring a palindrome?'.

followupVariations.title: Perfect Squares
followupVariations.hint: Partition a number instead of a string — minimize pieces (squares) rather than test existence.

patternNote: Canonical prefix-partition Dynamic Programming over a hash-set dictionary. Recognize it whenever a sequence must be split into pieces from a fixed set and a prefix is valid iff an earlier prefix is valid plus one allowed chunk. Same skeleton as Word Break II, Palindrome Partitioning, and Concatenated Words.
